newsitem.title: USA: Report says U.S. didn't press Swiss -- CNN.
newsitem.headline: Report says U.S. didn't press Swiss -- CNN.

text.p: A new U.S. study to be released on Wednesday is expected to criticize both the Swiss and American governments for their handling of Nazi gold after the Second World War, a television report said on Tuesday.

Marvin Hier, dean and founder of the Simon Wiesenthal Center, a Jewish human rights agency, told Reuters, meanwhile, that the German government had given him word that it would research what happened to the personal wealth of hundreds of leading Nazis after the war.

The new U.S. study, which deals with gold the Nazis looted from occupied countries and Holocaust victims, will be made public on Wednesday by Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat and the State Department's chief historian, William Slaney, who compiled it.
CNN said on Tuesday the document faults the United States for not pushing Switzerland hard enough to account for and return the gold it had acquired in financial deals with the Nazis during the war.
The study also criticizes Switzerland for using its neutrality to "advance their own economic self-interest even after it became apparent that the allies would win," CNN said, quoting the study.

State Department spokesman John Dinger declined to comment on the study before its official release. A State Department official also warned against early "leaks" of the report, saying they may be based on inaccurate or incomplete information.
A Swiss embassy spokeswoman also declined comment, saying the embassy would have a news conference on Wednesday.
Sources close to the State Department told Reuters last week the report would be very harsh on the Swiss role in the war as bankers and even money-launderers for the Third Reich.

Hier, speaking by telephone from New York, said he was pursuing another angle he did not expect the Eizenstat report to cover. "What happened to the fabulous wealth available to the leading Nazis that was never found?" he said.

He said he had submitted a list of 334 names of senior Nazi officials to the German government who may have transferred their wealth to neutral countries like Switzerland and received an answer from the German Finance Ministry last week that it would research the matter.
Noting the search for assets of Holocaust victims, Hier said, "if the victims accounts have an estimated $32 million, I can assure you the perpetrators' accounts would have many millions more."
"Some of the money may have been earned from slave labor campaigns, or confiscated from Jews. That money belongs to the victims of the Holocaust," he said.
A German embassy spokesman in Washington could not be reached for comment on Tuesday evening.
The Eizenstat report involved the work of 11 government agencies and draws on more than 15 million documents, including thousands of documents that were declassified for the first time, Dinger said.

On Sunday, Eizenstat told thousands of Holocaust survivors in New York that the report would pull no punches, saying: "This report will be objective. It will be fair and it will be tough in not only revealing the role of the neutrals but also shining the spotlight on the U.S. government."
Eizenstat has played a key role in negotiating the return of properties confiscated from Jewish victims of Nazi Germany to Holocaust survivors and their families.
